idea_name: Row-Free Weed Segmentation for Non-Row-Planted Tropical Smallholdings
one_sentence_pitch: For agronomists advising broadcast-sown Southeast Asian smallholder rice and vegetable plots, current UAV weed-segmentation models silently rely on crop-row geometry as a hidden prior, and this project measures and removes that dependency with a row-free density/context model, quantifying exactly how much published accuracy evaporates when the row assumption is false.
problem_statement: Public UAV crop/weed segmentation datasets and several published methods (RoWeeder, CRowNet-style row detectors, aerial crop-row pressure mapping) either train on row-planted European/Australian mechanised fields (sugar beet in WeedMap and PhenoBench, maize in WeedsGalore and BAWSeg) or explicitly exploit row geometry as a computational shortcut to build pseudo-labels or localise weeds (inter-row = weed, intra-row = crop). Southeast Asian and Singapore smallholder plots are frequently broadcast-sown, direct-seeded, or intercropped with irregular spacing -- most Mekong Delta rice (the dominant SEA staple) is direct-seeded/broadcast, not transplanted in rows, and Singapore's small rooftop/vertical farms similarly lack row geometry. When the row prior is false, row-dependent methods have no defined fallback: a published crop-row detector (Moldvai et al. 2025, Agronomy) documents its own failure mode -- it cannot determine row direction under heavy weed pressure and silently produces misleading output. No public method or dataset currently quantifies how much of published weed-segmentation performance is actually attributable to the row assumption, nor offers a validated substitute for the non-row case.
proposed_technical_approach: Two linked experiments on the same base architecture (a lightweight encoder-decoder segmentation network, e.g. SegFormer-B0 or a MobileNetV3/UNet hybrid, RGB+NIR input where available): (1) Controlled row-prior ablation -- take a row-planted dataset (WeedMap or PhenoBench), synthetically destroy row alignment by jittering/rotating plant-instance positions within the same images (preserving crop/weed class ratios and local density) to create matched row vs. de-rowed versions of the same data, then compare a row-prior-exploiting baseline (re-implementation of RoWeeder's pseudo-label generation) against a row-free model on both versions -- isolating the row-prior contribution without confounding it with a crop-type domain shift. (2) Cross-domain generalization test -- train row-based baselines on WeedMap/PhenoBench and evaluate zero-shot on a genuinely non-row public dataset (the Mekong Delta weedy-rice UAV dataset, broadcast/direct-seeded), quantifying the accuracy drop. The row-free model replaces explicit row-position features with (a) a learned plant-instance density map (auxiliary head predicting local plant count per patch, supervised from instance masks) and (b) a spatial-context encoder (dilated/non-local attention over the tile) that captures crop-weed co-occurrence statistics without assuming periodicity. Loss: combined cross-entropy segmentation loss + density-map MSE auxiliary loss. Training/inference entirely on UAV RGB(+multispectral) orthomosaic tiles; no drone flight required by the student.

labels_and_ground_truth: WeedMap, PhenoBench and WeedsGalore provide expert-annotated pixel-level crop/weed/background masks (plus PhenoBench leaf instances). The Mekong weedy-rice dataset's polygon masks were generated by a fine-tuned Segment Anything Model and then reviewed/corrected by experts (semi-automated, not fully manual) -- this is a real risk: label noise/boundary imprecision from SAM-assisted annotation could be misread as row-prior model failure unless carefully audited. The synthetic row-jittering ablation (destroying row alignment on an already-labelled row dataset) sidesteps this risk for the controlled experiment, since ground truth masks are preserved and only spatial arrangement is perturbed.

evaluation_protocol: Primary metric: weed IoU / mean IoU (matching WeedMap/RoWeeder convention) and F1, on held-out test tiles. Success criterion: (1) on the synthetic row-jittered ablation, quantify the IoU/F1 delta between row-prior-exploiting baseline and the row-free model as row alignment is progressively destroyed (0% to 100% jitter) -- a defensible result shows the row-exploiting baseline's performance degrades sharply (e.g. >15-20 F1 points) while the row-free model degrades much less; (2) on the cross-domain test, evaluate models trained on WeedMap/PhenoBench zero-shot on the Mekong weedy-rice dataset and report the absolute IoU/F1 drop versus in-domain performance, then show the row-free model narrows that gap. Geographic generalisation is measured directly by the EU/Australia-trained-to-SEA-tested transfer; temporal generalisation is secondary (WeedsGalore's multitemporal splits can be reused if time permits).
novelty_delta: This is NOT 'applied weed segmentation to Southeast Asia' -- the region does not merely relocate an existing pipeline, it breaks a load-bearing assumption that several published methods (RoWeeder explicitly, and the row-pressure-mapping literature) rely on to generate training signal or localise weeds at all. No paper found in this search (arXiv cs.CV sweep 2023-2026, OpenAlex/Crossref/dblp sweep) performs a controlled ablation isolating the row-prior's contribution to reported weed-segmentation accuracy, nor benchmarks row-trained models zero-shot against a genuinely non-row/broadcast-sown public UAV dataset. The technical delta is twofold: (a) a clean experimental design (synthetic row-jittering on the same images) that isolates the row-prior variable from confounding crop-type/domain shift, which as far as this search could determine has not been done; (b) a density/context-prior architecture proposed as a working substitute, evaluated for whether it actually survives row removal rather than just documenting that removal hurts. The 'defensible delta' per H1 is best read as new data regime (row vs. non-row planting geometry) plus a measurable comparison against RoWeeder's published F1=75.3 on WeedMap under both original and de-rowed conditions.
prior_art_that_threatens_it: RoWeeder (De Marinis et al., ECCV 2024 workshops, arXiv:2410.04983) is the closest prior art: it explicitly builds its entire training signal from crop-row detection, so it is simultaneously the best baseline to interrogate and evidence that the row prior is already known to be load-bearing in the literature -- but it does not test what happens when rows are absent, so it does not pre-empt this project. Moldvai et al. 2025 (Agronomy, 10.3390/agronomy15081762) independently documents crop-row detectors failing under heavy weed pressure, which is adjacent evidence but not a segmentation-accuracy ablation. VL-WS (Vision-Language Semantic Grounding for Multi-Domain Crop-Weed Segmentation, arXiv:2602.23677, 2026) targets cross-domain generalisation across ground+UAV imagery and four benchmark datasets, which is conceptually adjacent (domain-invariant representations) but its stated benchmark datasets are still European/mechanised-field sources as far as could be determined here [uncertain -- could not fully enumerate its four benchmark datasets from the abstract alone; if any of them are non-row, this narrows the novelty gap and should be checked before committing]. No 2024-2026 paper found explicitly frames 'row-prior ablation' or 'non-row generalization' as its research question.
h2_generic_check: Core is semantic/instance segmentation with an explicit bias-ablation study, not a chatbot, dashboard, leaf-classifier, NDVI viewer, tabular yield model, or a rerun of an existing crop-type benchmark -- passes the 8 banned-pattern check. Could the one-sentence summary describe 50 other FYPs? No, provided the ablation design (synthetic row-jittering to isolate the prior, plus explicit zero-shot non-row test with a named F1 number to beat) is retained in the pitch; a naive 'weed segmentation with a drone in Malaysia' framing would fail this test, so the write-up must foreground the bias-ablation angle, not the segmentation task itself.
user_segment: Primary: agronomists and extension officers at Vietnamese Mekong Delta rice cooperatives who advise smallholder farmers practising direct-seeded/broadcast rice cultivation (the dominant establishment method for ~69-100% of Mekong Delta rice farmers per multiple agronomy sources), who need weed pressure maps but are currently underserved by row-dependent tools. Secondary/demo: Singapore small-plot/rooftop urban farm operators and their agronomic advisors, where intercropping and irregular spacing similarly break the row assumption (per N1(a) in the brief).
quantified_pain: Weed infestation in direct-seeded rice (the exact non-row establishment method this project targets) can reduce yield by up to 50% (Shekhawat, Rathore & Chauhan 2020, Agronomy, DOI 10.3390/agronomy10091264). A closely related figure: weed pressure in forage corn causes yield losses of up to 31.5% (USU-Corn-WeedDB, arXiv:2606.06709, 2026). These are the best directly-citable numbers found; a Mekong-Delta-specific weedy-rice yield-loss percentage could not be retrieved in this session (the 2016 Crop Protection paper on weedy rice in the Mekong Delta was paywalled) [uncertain -- flagged, not fabricated].

demo_artifact: Live laptop demo: load a held-out UAV tile from the Mekong weedy-rice dataset (genuinely non-row/broadcast), run both the RoWeeder-style row-prior baseline and the row-free density/context model side by side, and show the row-prior baseline producing visibly wrong/empty row-structured output (because there is no row to detect) while the row-free model produces a sensible weed mask -- a visual, intuitive 'here is a published method silently failing, and here is what fixes it' moment that a CS panel can grasp in under 2 minutes without needing domain agronomy knowledge.
build_vs_research_ratio: Approximately 65:35 engineering:research. Engineering: the synthetic row-jittering ablation pipeline, a working segmentation model with a density-map auxiliary head, a reproduction of RoWeeder's row-detection pseudo-labelling as the baseline, and a demo interface. Research: designing the controlled ablation so it isolates the row-prior variable cleanly, and interpreting cross-dataset generalisation results without over-claiming causality.
publication_venue_fit: ECCV CVPPA workshop (where RoWeeder itself and PhenoBench-adjacent work were published) is the most natural fit given the direct engagement with RoWeeder as baseline; IGARSS or Remote Sensing MDPI are plausible alternates given the dataset-bias-audit framing has broad remote-sensing-methodology appeal.
key_risks: 1. (Method risk, highest) The synthetic row-jittering ablation must be designed carefully -- naive jittering could inadvertently change local density statistics or create implausible plant overlaps, confounding the row-prior isolation; this needs careful validation before trusting any delta numbers.

2. (Data-label risk) The Mekong weedy-rice dataset's masks are SAM-generated-then-corrected, not fully manual, and its 'non-row' status is inferred from regional agronomy literature rather than stated explicitly in the dataset paper -- if inspection of the actual imagery shows more row structure than expected (some Mekong Delta farmers do use drum-seeders which impose faint row-like patterns), the core premise weakens.

3. (Prior-art risk) VL-WS's exact four benchmark datasets were not fully enumerated in this session; if one of them turns out to already be non-row, the novelty claim needs tightening before committing engineering time.

4. (Evaluation risk) Cross-domain zero-shot transfer conflates row-prior loss with crop-type domain shift (sugar beet/maize to rice) and sensor differences (RedEdge/Sequoia to Mavic 3M multispectral) -- the paper's central claim depends on the synthetic ablation (risk 1) to isolate the row variable cleanly, since the cross-dataset test alone cannot do so.

5. (Scope risk) A fully convincing row-prior-ablation study plus a working row-free model plus a credible demo is a substantial scope for one FYP; the density/context-prior architecture may need to be simplified (e.g. drop the context-attention branch and keep only the density head) if time runs short in the final weeks.
kill_criteria: Week 1: Download WeedMap, PhenoBench, WeedsGalore and the Mekong weedy-rice dataset; visually inspect the Mekong imagery directly -- if it shows clear row/drum-seeder structure rather than broadcast irregularity, the core premise fails and the idea should be abandoned or re-scoped to a different non-row dataset.

Week 1-2: Re-implement RoWeeder's row-detection pseudo-label generator and reproduce its published F1=75.3 on WeedMap within a reasonable tolerance (e.g. +/-5 points) -- if this cannot be reproduced, the baseline-comparison plan needs a fallback (e.g. a simpler row-exploiting heuristic).

Week 2: Build the synthetic row-jittering pipeline and sanity-check on a small subset that jittering measurably destroys detectable row periodicity (e.g. via autocorrelation/FFT peak analysis) without changing per-tile plant density -- if jittering cannot be made clean, the controlled-ablation design (this project's main novelty claim) is compromised.

Week 3-4: Run the first ablation pass (baseline vs row-free model, row vs de-rowed) on WeedMap alone -- if the row-exploiting baseline does NOT show a meaningfully larger degradation than the row-free model, the central hypothesis may be false and the project should pivot to reporting that negative result honestly rather than forcing a positive one.

hard_constraint_verdict.H1: PASS - genuine gap identified: no found paper isolates the row-prior's contribution via controlled ablation or benchmarks row-trained models zero-shot on a real non-row dataset; RoWeeder gives a concrete named baseline/number to interrogate.
hard_constraint_verdict.H2: PASS with caution - not a banned pattern, but only if the write-up foregrounds the bias-ablation framing rather than presenting as 'yet another weed segmentation model'.
hard_constraint_verdict.H3: PASS - UAV RGB/multispectral imagery is the sole model input throughout.
hard_constraint_verdict.H4: PASS - named user segment is Mekong Delta rice cooperative agronomists (direct-seeded/broadcast rice smallholders), with Singapore small-plot/intercropped farms as a secondary demo angle per N1(a).
hard_constraint_verdict.H5: PASS - all four datasets are free and small (~15-20GB total for MVE), models are lightweight, training fits comfortably in 24GB/MPS and well under 12-hour runs; no drone flight required.
hard_constraint_verdict.H6: PASS - the demo (baseline visibly fails on non-row imagery, row-free model succeeds) is a strong, intuitive 60-second pitch for a CS panel.

overall_recommendation: STRONG. This candidate identifies a real, verifiable structural bias in the published weed-segmentation literature (RoWeeder's row-dependence, WeedMap/PhenoBench/WeedsGalore's row-planted training data) and pairs it with a genuinely non-row public dataset (Mekong Delta weedy rice, CC-BY, freely accessible) that substitutes for flying a drone, satisfying H5's no-own-drone constraint. The main execution risk is designing the row-prior isolation ablation rigorously rather than the segmentation model itself, which is a research-design risk rather than a feasibility risk.
confidence: Medium-High. Confidence would rise to High with: (a) direct visual/quantitative confirmation that the Mekong weedy-rice dataset imagery is actually non-row (autocorrelation/FFT check), since this was inferred from regional agronomy statistics rather than stated in the dataset paper itself; (b) full enumeration of VL-WS's four benchmark datasets to rule out an existing non-row test already in the literature; (c) a successful reproduction of RoWeeder's published F1 as a sanity check on the re-implementation.
